::: {.why}
It is the only execution metric that charges you for not trading, which is why it is the honest one and why algorithms optimised against VWAP can look good while losing money.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Decompose implementation shortfall into its standard components including opportunity cost.
- Say what it captures that VWAP slippage does not, with an example where the two disagree.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>60 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [35 min]{.task-min} Implement the decomposition in qlib/exec/shortfall.py: the difference between the decision price and the achieved price, split into delay cost, trading cost against the arrival price, and the opportunity cost of the unfilled quantity valued at the closing price. Assert the components sum to the total.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Construct the disagreement: a passive algorithm that fills only when the price comes to it will beat VWAP on the fills it gets and will fail to fill when the price runs away, which is exactly when not filling is most expensive. Simulate that case and report both metrics to show the divergence.
:::
:::

## The running strategy

::: {.project}
qlib/exec/shortfall.py measures implementation shortfall with opportunity cost included and its components reconciling to the total, which becomes the standard execution metric for the paper account in phase 10.
:::
